q: What does natural language processing focus on?
options: Deriving meaning from human language and handling it automatically
Compressing large text files so they take up much less storage space on a disk drive
Recognising objects and their positions in photographs
Checking that program source code follows a set grammar
explain: NLP is a branch of machine learning and AI that derives meaning from human language and handles it automatically. It covers both speech and text.

q: Which task is natural language generation?
options: Reading a customer review carefully and working out what the writer actually means by it
Taking a formal logic statement and expressing it in natural language
Splitting a sentence into individual word tokens
Removing hashtags and HTML tags from a message
explain: Generation goes from a formal statement to natural language. Understanding goes the other way, from a sentence to what it means.

q: Which of these are uses of NLP?
options: Sentiment analysis of customer reviews
Identifying fake news
Machine translation
Spam message detection
Edge detection in an image
explain: Sentiment analysis, fake news detection, translation and spam detection all work on language. Edge detection works on pixels, so it belongs to image processing.

q: What is the purpose of text preparation and cleaning before NLP?
options: To translate the text into a second language before analysis
To improve the quality of raw text so it can be analysed better
To add extra words to short documents so they all match in length
To label each message as spam or ham by hand before training
explain: Preprocessing improves the quality of raw text for analysis. Its tasks include removing irrelevant characters, lowercasing, tokenization and removing stop words.

q: Which of these are text preparation tasks?
options: Removing irrelevant characters
Lowercasing
Tokenization
Removing stop words
Max pooling
explain: Removing irrelevant characters, lowercasing, tokenization and stop word removal are all cleaning steps. Max pooling is a CNN layer from Week 8.

q:
After cleaning, what does "

Hey there!!!

#Excited" become?
options: Hey there Excited

Hey there

Excited

Hey there

#Excited, with the tags left in place
Hey there!!! #Excited
explain: Cleaning removes HTML tags, punctuation and hashtag symbols but keeps the words. Lowercasing is a separate step.

q: Why is case normalisation applied to text for sentiment analysis?
options: Capital letters always signal a strong positive sentiment, so the model needs them kept exactly as written
Casing gives little relevant information, so removing it reduces irrelevant variety
Lowercase words are shorter, so the model trains on fewer characters
Neural networks can only read lowercase letters, so capitals cause errors
explain: Casing does not really tell the model about sentiment. Turning "CASH" and "cash" into one form reduces irrelevant variety in the data.

q: What counts as an outlier in NLP?
options: Any word that appears in more than one document anywhere in the training corpus
Unusual or extreme words, phrases or documents that do not fit the usual distribution
The words that carry the very strongest positive or negative sentiment anywhere in the whole corpus of documents
Every message that is labelled as spam in the training data
explain: Outliers are unusual or extreme words, phrases or documents. One approach is to drop the bottom 20% of words.

q: What is tokenization?
options: Splitting text into units such as words, subwords or characters
Reducing each word to its root by cutting off suffixes
Replacing every word with a number that counts how often it appears
Removing common words such as "and" and "the" from a sentence
explain: Tokenization splits sentences into tokens. The level can be words, subwords or characters, depending on the granularity needed.

q: What is an n-gram?
options: A contiguous sequence of N words or tokens
A word that appears exactly N times in a document
A dense vector with N values that stands for one word
A list of the N most common stop words in a language
explain: An n-gram is N tokens in a row. N-grams capture context and which words occur together.

q: Why are stop words removed?
options: They are spelling mistakes and typos that confuse the model during training
They are common words such as "and" and "the" that add little meaning
They are the rarest words, so the model cannot learn them
They always carry negative sentiment and bias the model
explain: Stop words are common words that do not contribute to the sentiment. They are filtered out before the text reaches the model.

q: What does stemming do to a word?
options: Swaps it for a synonym that has the same meaning in the sentence
Reduces it to a root by removing suffixes and prefixes
Turns it into a dense vector of continuous values
Splits it into its individual characters
explain: Stemming cuts prefixes and suffixes so variations of a word are treated as one. Happily and happiness both become happi.

q: What is the lemma of "went"?
options: Wen
Went
Go
Going
explain: Lemmatization gives the dictionary form and uses meaning, so went maps to go. A stemmer works on spelling and cannot make that link.
flag: The slides say stemming uses heuristics. That a stemmer cannot map went to go is an inference from that.

q: Which statement compares stemming and lemmatization correctly?
options: Stemming uses context and always gives a valid dictionary word, while lemmatization just cuts letters off the end by rule
Lemmatization uses context and gives valid base forms, while stemming uses heuristics and can give non-words
Both always give exactly the same output for every word in the text
Lemmatization only removes prefixes, while stemming only removes suffixes
explain: Lemmatization keeps meaning and returns real words called lemmas. Stemming follows rules of thumb, so happily can become happi, which is not a word.

q: Why is text vectorised before it goes into a machine learning model?
options: Models do maths on numbers, so text must become numerical vectors
Vectors take up less memory than the original text in every case
Vectorization removes the stop words and punctuation automatically
It translates the text into English before the model sees it
explain: Vectorization turns text into numerical vectors. Maths is easier on numbers, so algorithms can then process the text.

q: Which of these are vectorization techniques?
options: Bag of words
TF-IDF
One-hot encoding
Stemming
Tokenization
explain: Bag of words, TF-IDF and one-hot encoding turn text into numbers. Stemming and tokenization are cleaning steps that come before.

q: What does a TF-IDF score try to show?
options: How long a document is compared with the rest of the corpus
How important a word is to one document within a collection of documents
Whether a single word in the text carries a positive or a negative sentiment overall
How similar two words are in meaning
explain: TF-IDF reflects how important a word is to a document in a corpus. A word frequent in one document but rare across the corpus scores high.
flag: The slides give only the definition. Why a word that is rare across the corpus scores high is standard textbook reasoning.

q: A corpus has 200 documents and the term "aid" appears in 8 of them. The document "aid people health driv" has 4 terms. What is the TF-IDF of "aid" in that document?
options: About 0.80
About 3.21
About 0.25
About 25.0
explain: TF is 1 / 4 = 0.25. IDF is ln(200 / 8) = 3.21. TF-IDF is 0.25 x 3.21, which is about 0.80.

q: How do word embeddings differ from TF-IDF vectors?
options: Embeddings are sparse vectors built from raw term counts, while TF-IDF gives dense vectors of continuous values that capture meaning
Embeddings are dense vectors of continuous values that capture meaning, while TF-IDF gives sparse vectors
Embeddings can only be used for images, while TF-IDF is used for text
Embeddings keep the original words, while TF-IDF turns them into numbers
explain: Embeddings are dense, continuous vectors that place related words close together. TF-IDF gives sparse vectors based on term frequencies.

q: Which of these are pre-trained word embedding models?
options: Word2Vec
GloVe
FastText
TF-IDF
YOLO
explain: Word2Vec, GloVe and FastText learn vectors from word use in very large corpora. TF-IDF is a frequency statistic and YOLO is an object detector from Week 9.

q: In the example embeddings, why are the vectors for "king" and "queen" close together?
options: They happen to have the same number of letters, so their vectors line up
They are used in similar contexts, so they have a related meaning
They both appear only once in the text
The model gives every noun the same vector
explain: Embeddings capture semantic relationships from context. King [0.4, 0.7, -0.1] and queen [0.5, 0.8, -0.2] are close because their meanings are related.

q: What is the problem with a model that only uses word frequencies?
options: It ignores word order, which can change the meaning of a sentence
It cannot handle any document that is longer than about ten words in total
It needs labelled images as well as text to train
It always predicts the spam class for every message
explain: Frequencies say which words appear but not in what order. Order matters for meaning, so a sequential model such as an RNN is used.

q: Why is "That car is sick" hard for a sentiment model?
options: The sentence is far too short to be tokenized into words by the model
"Sick" can be positive or negative, so context decides the sentiment
It contains a stop word that cannot be removed
Cars are not covered in the training vocabulary
explain: In slang, sick can be praise. The model needs context to tell the positive reading from the negative one.
flag: The slide shows the sentence as either positive or negative. Reading sick as slang praise is an inference.

q: What does texts_to_sequences do before an RNN or LSTM is trained?
options: Turns each text into a sequence of numbers that keeps the word order
Sorts all the words in each text into alphabetical order before training starts
Counts how many documents contain each word
Removes every word that appears fewer than twice
explain: RNNs expect sequential data. texts_to_sequences replaces each word with a number and keeps the words in their original order.
flag: The slides name the function but do not say how it works. Mapping each word to an integer index is how the Keras tokenizer does it.

q: Why are sequences padded before they go into an LSTM?
options: Padding removes the rare words from the vocabulary so the model has fewer to learn
The network needs input of the same shape, but texts have different lengths
Padding adds the sentiment label to the end of each sequence
Padding converts each word into a dense vector
explain: Texts give sequences of different lengths. pad_sequences pads or truncates them to one fixed length so the network gets the same shape every time.

q: What problem does an embedding layer solve?
options: Sparse representations such as one-hot encoding are inefficient
The sequences have different lengths, so each one must be padded to match the others
Words are in mixed case and need lowercasing
The model forgets early words because of vanishing gradients
explain: One-hot vectors are long and mostly zero. The embedding layer turns words into dense, low-dimensional vectors that capture meaning and cut computation.

q: Explain what natural language processing is and give three of its uses.
model: Natural language processing is a branch of machine learning and artificial intelligence. It focuses on deriving meaning from human language and handling it automatically. It covers both speech and text. Uses include chatbots, sentiment analysis of reviews or social media, fake news detection, translation, question answering, summarising and speech recognition.
points: Branch of machine learning or AI
Derives meaning from human language and handles it automatically
Covers speech and text
Gives three uses such as chatbots, sentiment analysis or translation

q: Explain the difference between natural language understanding and natural language generation.
model: Natural language understanding takes a sentence and works out what it means, for example reading a review to find its sentiment. Natural language generation goes the other way. It takes a formal logic statement and expresses it in natural language. Both are parts of NLP.
points: Understanding takes a sentence and works out its meaning
Generation takes a formal statement and expresses it in natural language
They work in opposite directions
Gives an example of either

q: Describe the main steps used to prepare raw text before it is given to an NLP model.
model: Text preparation improves the quality of raw text. First, irrelevant characters such as punctuation, hashtags, HTML tags and encoding symbols are removed. Case normalisation turns all text to lowercase, since casing adds little meaning. Tokenization splits sentences into tokens such as words. Stop words like and, to and the are removed. Stemming or lemmatization then reduces words to a common form.
points: Removes irrelevant characters such as punctuation or HTML tags
Lowercases the text
Tokenizes the text into words or other units
Removes stop words
Applies stemming or lemmatization

q: Explain tokenization and n-grams, and why tokenization matters for an NLP model.
model: Tokenization splits sentences into tokens. These are usually words but can be subwords or characters, depending on the granularity needed. It matters because it turns raw text into a form a machine learning model can process and analyse. N-grams are contiguous sequences of N tokens. They capture context and which words occur together.
points: Splits text into tokens
Tokens can be words, subwords or characters
Turns raw text into a form a model can process
N-grams are sequences of N tokens in a row that capture context

q: Compare stemming and lemmatization, with an example of each.
model: Stemming reduces a word to its root by removing prefixes and suffixes, using heuristics. It can give non-words, for example happily and happiness both become happi. Lemmatization turns a word into its dictionary form and considers context and meaning. It always gives a valid word, for example went becomes go and better becomes good. Both bring variants of a word to a common form.
points: Stemming removes prefixes and suffixes using heuristics
Stemming can produce non-words, for example happi
Lemmatization uses context and meaning to give the dictionary form
Gives a lemma example such as went to go or better to good

q: Explain how TF-IDF works, and calculate it for a term that appears once in a 4-term document, where 8 of the 200 documents in the corpus contain the term.
model: TF-IDF is a statistic that shows how important a word is to a document within a corpus. Term frequency is how often the term appears in the document divided by the number of terms, here 1 / 4 = 0.25. Inverse document frequency is the log of the number of documents over the number containing the term, here ln(200 / 8) = 3.21. TF-IDF multiplies them, giving 0.25 x 3.21, about 0.80. Each document then becomes a vector of these numbers.
points: Shows how important a word is to a document in a corpus
TF-IDF is TF x IDF, about 0.80

q: Explain what word embeddings are and how they differ from TF-IDF.
model: An embedding is a special type of vectorisation. Each word becomes a dense vector of continuous values in a vector space. The vectors capture semantic relationships, so words used in similar contexts such as king and queen get similar vectors. Pre-trained models such as Word2Vec, GloVe and FastText learn them from very large corpora. TF-IDF instead gives sparse vectors based on term frequencies.
points: Words become dense vectors of continuous values
Vectors capture meaning, so related words are close
Names a model such as Word2Vec, GloVe or FastText
TF-IDF gives sparse frequency-based vectors

q: Explain why a frequency-based model is not enough for sentiment analysis, and how text is prepared for an RNN instead.
model: A model built on word frequencies ignores the order of words, but order matters for meaning. Context also decides sentiment, for example sick in that car is sick can be praise. RNNs such as LSTMs and GRUs process sequential data and keep context. The text is turned into sequences of numbers with texts_to_sequences. Since RNNs need fixed-size input, pad_sequences pads or truncates each one to the same length. An embedding layer then turns words into dense vectors.
points: Frequency models ignore word order, which affects meaning
RNNs, LSTMs or GRUs keep the order and context
Text is converted to sequences, for example with texts_to_sequences
Sequences are padded or truncated to a fixed length
An embedding layer gives dense word vectors
